newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. opposition against huge Canada gas pipe seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposition against huge Canada gas pipe seen.

text.p: A group of Canadian natural gas producers aiming to build a C$3.6-billion pipeline to Chicago from Northern Canada can expect opposition from U.S. oil companies and governments, a natural gas consultant said on Monday.
"It would surprise me if there were not," Mark Perry of Tulsa-based Windward Consulting Services told reporters following a presentation to a pipeline conference.

Alliance Pipeline, a consortium of 18 Canadian companies aiming to build the 1.25 billion cubic feet per day line, is in the midst of an open season to attracting shipping commitments for the project. Under current plans, it would be on stream in 1999.

Perry said the pipeline, which when coupled with an expansion in 1998 of the Northern Border Partners LP pipeline, would flood the Chicago market with Canadian gas, driving prices down and lowering returns for U.S. producers.

Most U.S. producers that would oppose the project would do so officially through the Independent Petroleum Association of America, which would file strong protest during Alliance's regulatory proceedings in the U.S., said Perry.
Perry, detailing his bias, said he has acted for various producers operating in the Lower 48 states.

Like others that have registered their opposition to Alliance, he cited the example of California, which became flooded with natural gas after major pipeline expansions from Canada and the San Juan Basin in the U.S. Southwest in the early 1990s.
Gas prices have been much lower in California than in the U.S. Gulf Coast or Midwest regions.
Also, when the Mojave and Pacific Gas Transmission expansions were built, the result was $500,000 in stranded costs on existing lines that had to be bankrolled by the industry, he said.

It meant the consumer in the end was unable to reap the benefits of lower gas prices, Perry said. "What happens is the commodity component, as a percentage of the total cost of your gas supply goes down," he said.

Today, the existing lines, El Paso and Transwestern, move some of their gas east from the San Juan Basin, much of it ending up in Chicago, he said, so that would possibly be displaced with Gulf Coast supply because of Alliance, he said.

The possibility of displaced supply and lower revenues would likely anger the governments of Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and New Mexico, which rely on oil and gas revenues for their livelihoods, he said.
"You start squeezing that and you won't have to worry about the producers, it will be the state government that shows up."
However, with oil prices currently increasing opposition will not likely be mounting in the next few months, he said.

Alliance, which includes such firms as Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, Alberta Energy Co Ltd and IPL Energy Inc, has said the wide gulf between Canadian and U.S. gas prices would narrow if the project went ahead.
The lack of export pipeline capacity and resulting glut within Alberta's borders has often been blamed for depressed Canadian gas prices.
David Manning, president of the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers, said the line would likely mean lower Midwest prices and higher Canadian prices.
He said his organization, which represents most of Canada's producers, supports projects that are market-driven and deemed as economic. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
